summary: Describes an optional extension to IS-IS that adds checksums to CSNP and PSNP packets. The original protocol relied on lower layers to detect corruption, but experience showed this does not always hold. IS-IS is a link-state interior routing protocol used by ISPs.

eli5.summary: Routers pass notes about the network to each other, and sometimes notes get smudged. This adds a seal that lets receivers notice if one was damaged.

questions: what is the is-is optional checksum
subtitle: Adding integrity checks to IS-IS routing protocol packets.

tldr.problem: ISIS, a link-state routing protocol used by ISPs, originally relied on underlying network layers to detect data corruption, but experience showed this assumption did not always hold, leading to undetected corrupted routing information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3358 defines an optional TLV (Type-Length-Value) field that carries a Fletcher checksum over the complete ISIS packet. Routers implementing optional checksums verify the checksum and discard corrupted packets, while routers without checksum support can still process the packet.
tldr.outcome: The optional checksum extension lets ISIS deployments add a data integrity layer without breaking compatibility with existing routers, protecting against corruption from faulty hardware or protocols that lack their own checksums.

today: RFC 3358 extends IS-IS with optional data integrity checks. IS-IS remains in use by ISPs for routing, and the optional checksum feature allows modern deployments to add extra protection against corruption without requiring all routers on the network to be upgraded simultaneously.

sections.title: Optional Checksums in ISIS
sections.content:
IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) is an interior gateway routing protocol used by ISPs to determine how to forward packets within their networks. It is a link-state protocol, meaning routers exchange information about the network topology with each other. ISIS originally did not include checksums in its PDUs (protocol data units); instead it relied on the underlying data-link layer to verify data integrity. In practice, however, some network technologies lack checksums, and faulty hardware implementations can introduce corruption that goes undetected.

RFC 3358 extends ISIS with an optional checksum field that protects CSNP (Complete Sequence Number PDU), PSNP (Partial Sequence Number PDU), and IIH (ISIS Hello) packets against corruption.
sections.eli5: ISIS is a protocol routers use to tell each other about the network. It trusted lower layers to catch errors, but sometimes errors slipped through, so this RFC adds a checksum to catch them.

sections.title: The Checksum TLV and Compatibility
sections.content: The optional checksum is carried in a TLV field with type number 12 and length 2, containing the computed checksum. An implementation that supports optional checksums MAY include the TLV in packets, but MUST accept packets without it. Implementations that receive a checksum TLV MUST discard the packet if the checksum is incorrect, but implementations without checksum support MUST still accept the packet and ignore the TLV. This backward compatibility ensures that mixed networks of old and new routers work correctly. Additionally, if a packet includes signatures (like HMAC or MD5) for authentication, the checksum should either be omitted or sent as zero to avoid interference with signature computation.
sections.eli5: The checksum is optional, so old routers that do not know about it can still read the packet. New routers check the seal and throw away smudged packets.

sections.title: Checksum Computation
sections.content: The checksum is a Fletcher checksum computed according to ISO 8859 over the complete PDU. To compute it correctly, the implementation adds the optional checksum TLV to the packet with an initial checksum value of zero, then computes the checksum over the modified packet. This approach ensures that the checksum includes itself in the computation. By special convention, an implementation MAY send a checksum value of zero, which is treated as correct. This flexibility allows implementations to signal that they did not compute a checksum while still being compatible with systems that require it.
sections.eli5: The checksum math works by going through the packet once and computing a number. If the packet gets corrupted, that number will be wrong, and routers know to discard it.
